poem:
I am a diesel-breathing serpent coiled at Peachtree & Ellis,  
hydraulic doors hissing like hidden incantations.  
My rubber soles grip asphalt runes,  
each curb a threshold to undercity realms  
where commuters become exiles of gravity.

You board beneath the flicker of a tired streetlamp,  
flesh and bone pressed to vinyl seats that hide secret hollows—  
escape routes inscribed in the metal ribs underneath.  
Your mirror reflects a world slipping sideways:  
faces etched with stories of flight,  
eyes that have learned to sing of disorder.

At Peachtree Center, the steering wheel is a wand  
wreathed in diesel mist.  
I carve intersections into a map of escape tunnels,  
a labyrinth of pavement whispers.  
The system does not give a damn—  
so we wage our freedom in each stoplight’s amber glare.  
Full of surprises, my engine growls a manifesto  
against the gray handshake of predictability.

Around Peachtree & North Avenue, beneath traffic signals’ blinking watch,  
concrete fractures bloom with bioluminescent moss—  
an uncanny forest breathing between tire grooves.  
Here, chaos is law, and every reflection in my side mirror  
is a gateway to a hidden cosmos.  

You lean close, press your palm to cold metal;  
you sense the revolt pulsing under my chassis.  
This is a networked earth that won’t be contained—  
a riot of wheels forging freedom  
on curbs, in cracks, in the heartbeat of the city.
